results.title: PYXIS 12K
results.credit_line: Courtesy Blackmagic Design, Major Partner of ACMI
results.brief_description:
The Blackmagic PYXIS 12K is a compact box camera designed for flexibility. Made from precision CNC-machined aerospace aluminium, it is lightweight, strong and highly riggable. It can be mounted to drones, built into larger camera rigs, or adapted for documentary, commercial, feature film and personal projects.

Released in 2025, the PYXIS 12K brings high-resolution digital cinematography into a smaller, more customisable form. Its 12K sensor captures extremely detailed images, giving filmmakers more freedom to crop, stabilise or reframe footage. Its modular design allows filmmakers to shape the camera around each shoot, rather than working around a fixed camera body.

Its appeal lies in that combination: Hollywood-level resolution in a camera built for independent, professional and experimental workflows.

results.title: The Dance of the angels: ceramic sculptures of John Perceval
results.creator_credit: Tim Burstall, Patrick Ryan and Eltham Films
results.brief_description: Camera movement and film editing are combined to animate the ceramic figurines of John Perceval. He created his angels “more or less as symbols of the world’s survival.” An intangible element common to all Perceval’s angels is their spirit of humanity. These ceramic sculptures are disting- uished by their beautiful modelling, and their lustrous red copper glaze with its uncanny depth and beauty. Perceval does not devote himself exclusively to ceramic sculpture; he gives equal time to painting and has won the McCaughey and Vizard-Whollohan Prizes, and shared the Wynne Prize in 1961. Photography by Gerard Vanderberg; music by Dorian Le Gallienne.

results.title: City on the Swan
results.creator_credit: Norman A. Uren and Western Australian Government Film Unit
results.brief_description:
Promotional tourism film presented by the Western Australian Tourist Development Authority and produced by the Western Australian Government Film Unit. The film showcases Perth through its architecture, industry, transport, recreation and tourist attractions, presenting the city as a modern urban centre organised around the Swan River.

City scenes include St Georges Terrace, London Court, Wellington Street, the Hotel Adelphi, the Old Barracks, Narrows Bridge and Canning Bridge. Sequences at the General Post Office show radio telephone and postal services, while footage of factories and manufacturing includes porcelain and domestic pottery production, woodworking and the manufacture of period and modern furniture using plastics and metals.

The film follows Perth from the end of the working week into the weekend. On Friday evening, factory and city workers leave work as peak-hour traffic, buses and rail services carry commuters from the city to the suburbs and surrounding areas.

Saturday is presented through sport and recreation, including Australian rules football (footage of match between West Coast Eagles and North Melbourne teams), cricket, golf, rowing, motor racing, horse racing, water skiing (footage of women synchronised on skis) and the “novelty and brilliance of the marching girls”.
Tourist and civic sites include Queens Gardens with its Peter Pan statue, black swans at Hyde Park, the museum displays at the Old Mill in South Perth, (Princess) May Drive in Kings Park, and the University of Western Australia (footage of Winthrop Hall’s reflection pond and bust of Socrates). Also includes an excursion to Yanchep which features boating, gardens, swimming and afternoon tea.

Perth’s nightlife is represented through drive-in cinemas, including footage of projectionists at work, and the Ambassadors Theatre on Hay Street (demolished 1972).

On Sunday, focus returns to the Swan River, with fishing along Riverside Drive, speedboats and yacht racing on the river. The film concludes by promoting Perth as the “City on the Swan”, defined by the river, outdoor recreation and a relaxed metropolitan lifestyle (“Gentle and gracious, Perth makes its appeal with a delightful flare as the City on the Swan.”)

results.title: Long March: Restart
results.credit_line: Artwork courtesy of M+ Sigg Collection, Hong Kong. By donation.
results.brief_description:
Feng Mengbo transforms one of modern China’s defining political stories into a playable artwork.

This interactive adventure is inspired by the Long March, the Chinese Red Army’s military retreat of 1934–36. It unfolds as a side-scrolling videogame artwork across two giant screens. A Red Army soldier travels through an 8-bit world inspired by historical landmarks and retro games like Street Fighter II and Super Mario Bros. Armed with exploding Coca-Cola cans, he fights iconic characters, aliens and armies as revolutionary history and global pop culture collide.

Feng first imagined Long March: Restart in 1994 as a series of paintings. It took 14 years before custom software could support the interactive version completed in 2008. The title’s “restart” suggests both a videogame mechanic and a return to history. By remixing communist and capitalist symbols with videogame references, Feng asks how history is constructed, retold and replayed through the images and systems that surround us.

Play along, or watch as the soldier advances, and join the surreal, pixelated march through time and space.

results.title: Cyberthon VI: VAT
results.brief_description:
After the success of Spectrum, the Cyberthon artists were invited by Telstra to create a submission for an exhibition called The Edge, to be displayed at the Telstra Corporate Center on Exhibition Street. This demo was presented to Telstra at an annual meeting held at Dallas Brooks Hall.

The demo shows a CGI artists impression of the proposed ‘The Edge exhibition’ space as well as a simulation of the media submission process via the interactive Cyberthon VAT (V=Video, A=Audio, T=Text) porthole created using Deluxe Paint, with presentation edited in Scala on an Amiga 2000.

Animation loops that appear in simulated submission section were created by Ian Haig, Cyber Dada (Troy Innocent and Dale Nason), Don’t Shoot the Messenger (Steve Middleton & Attillio Gangemi), Tekno Mandala (Adem Jaffers), Julian Wong, Mish Fingers (Misha Hollenbach), Derek Shiel, Martine Corompt, and Force Fed (Stuart McCormick). Video camera footage was shot by Dale Nason from the back of a Chris Wrights moving van. 35mm still photographs were taken by Tao Wiess. Audio track was mixed by DJ Visitor (Andrew Till).

This work is part of the Cyberthon Archive, generously donated to ACMI by Adem Jaffers.

results.title: [Ted Parsons Home Movies: Reel 11]
results.brief_description:
Ted Parsons was a keen amateur filmmaker of the 1940s to 1960s. Ted’s films feature life in and around the Victorian regional city of Wangaratta post-war. This was a period of prosperity and optimism largely due to a successful textile industry that took Wangaratta from a small country town to major rural city, declared in 1959.

Ted captures the many sporting and social events, venues and clubs, holidays and travel along with scenes of everyday life. The collection also shows the broader issues faced by country people such as the regular flooding events around the Ovens and King Rivers.

Wangaratta’s success story as a manufacturing town traces the path of post-war migration and the accompanying growth of Australia’s economy, which makes these films particularly interesting.

The Ted Parsons Home Movie Collection has been donated to ACMI by the filmmaker’s grandson Barry Parsons. The films have been made on 16mm film.

This film shows scenes of a motor racing circuit. Ted films the cars from alongside the track, showing the dusty, mud-splattered action, as well as close-ups of the drivers, mechanics and race cars. The action throughout gives an insightful and exciting look at the sport.

A feature is a spectacular image of a burnt out car driving straight through a billboard set on fire.

results.brief_description:
Ted Parsons was a keen amateur filmmaker of the 1940s to 1960s. Ted’s films feature life in and around the Victorian regional city of Wangaratta post-war. This was a period of prosperity and optimism largely due to a successful textile industry that took Wangaratta from a small country town to major rural city, declared in 1959.

Ted captures the many sporting and social events, venues and clubs, holidays and travel along with scenes of everyday life. The collection also shows the broader issues faced by country people such as the regular flooding events around the Ovens and King Rivers.

The Ted Parsons Home Movie Collection has been donated to ACMI by the filmmaker’s grandson Barry Parsons. The films have been made on 16mm film.

This film captures some travels around Victoria. The Parsons take a trip from Wangaratta to Beechworth, down through Mount Buffalo to San Remo and Phillip Island on the south coast, and back up through the Dandenong Ranges and Healesville.

The film shows scenes of life in country towns of Victoria, including sporting and recreational events, the flooding of Ovens River, some beautiful footage of Phillip Island, the Australian Alps in autumn, and the Tesselaar Tulip Festival in Healesville.

The Parsons’ travels also take them to the Hume Dam, formerly known as the Hume Weir, which was a popular tourist destination during the 1940s and 50s.

A feature of the film is the flooded roads and paddocks of Wangaratta during the 1956 floods, which stemmed from major flooding in the Murray River.

Ted films road signs to indicate each stop on their travels.

results.brief_description:
Ted Parsons was a keen amateur filmmaker of the 1940s to 1960s. Ted’s films feature life in and around the Victorian regional city of Wangaratta post-war. This was a period of prosperity and optimism largely due to a successful textile industry that took Wangaratta from a small country town to major rural city, declared in 1959.

Ted captures the many sporting and social events, venues and clubs, holidays and travel along with scenes of everyday life. The collection also shows the broader issues faced by country people such as the regular flooding events around the Ovens and King Rivers.

Wangaratta’s success story as a manufacturing town traces the path of post-war migration and the accompanying growth of Australia’s economy, which makes these films particularly interesting.

The Ted Parsons Home Movie Collection has been donated to ACMI by the filmmaker’s grandson Barry Parsons. The films have been made on 16mm film.

This film captures the visit of Australian champion golfer Peter Thomson to the Wangaratta Golf Club in 1956. As shown by the poster in the film, Thomson teaches a golf clinic to an avid crowd. At the time, Thomson had won the British Open twice, and would go on to win it a total of five times - he was the first Australian golfer to win the championship and the only man to have won it in three consecutive years in the twentieth century (1954, 1955 and 1956).

The film shows off the lovely surrounds of the Golf Club set against the backdrop of the town itself and in particular, the backyards of houses. The golfers are particularly smartly dressed in clothes suitable for striding around the course with their golf bags and trolleys, the women in pleated or full mid calf skirts and the men tucking ties into shirts and full 1950s style trousers.

In this film, we can feel the atmosphere of Wangaratta in the post war period - a growing, prosperous community with an increasingly cosmopolitan outlook thanks to an influx of migrants to the area.

results.brief_description:
John Robert (Jack) Anderson (1924–1993) was a film distributor, cinema owner and photographer as well as an enthusiastic filmmaker in and around Ballarat in Victoria. Jack developed an interest in film very early at cinema shows and gained his first film experience while serving in WWII, photographing wartime conditions and aircraft involved in the defence of Australia’s north, including the aftermath of the Darwin bombing raid.

It was whilst working in photographic studios that Jack met his future wife, business partner and fellow film enthusiast Marie Bourke. Starting out by hiring films and showing them around regional Victoria, Jack and Marie established cinemas such as the Astor Cinema in Ararat, Bell Post Hill Drive-In in Geelong and the Southern and Northern Drive-Ins and Vegas 70 Cinema in Ballarat. In the 1970s, the Anderson family acquired and restored the Regent Theatre in Ballarat which would then become the first multiplex in regional Victoria.

Along the way, Jack filmed his family and friends activities and outings, horse racing, Ballarat street scenes, motorcycle scrambling and travel scenes on the road – an unusual and wonderful look at life in regional Victoria during the 1940s to the 1960s.

This film is all about the Anderson and Bourke families at home and out and about. The title cards introduce this film as being photographed by Jack but also directed by Marie Bourke (using her pre-married name). Marie has the family going about their everyday activities, sometimes surprising them with the camera and sometimes directing them to hold a pose. She films the family fishing, dining, cutting flowers and modelling their clothes. The family appear in their workday clothes as well as being dressed in their best.

This aspect of the film is a reminder of how people dressed in the 1940s to 1950s, when more expensive outfits were kept for outings such as church or shopping or special outings leaving working clothes for the day to day. It is a captivating look at the members of this extended family who obviously enjoyed each other’s company, their hometown of Ballarat and their individual pursuits and as always, there is a little comedy along the way.

This film was originally made using 9.5mm film.
